title: Exfiltration Over Physical Medium: Exfiltration over USB
shortTitle: Exfiltration Over Physical Medium: Exfiltration over USB
summary: This sub-technique covers data leaving an environment on removable USB storage rather than over a network path. It is the variant defenders meet in air-gapped or heavily segmented estates, where the adversary either brings a device in, plugs it into a host, stages the collected files onto it, and carries it out, or uses the device as a bridge between two systems that never talk to each other. The observable artefacts are host-side rather than network-side: device arrival and removal records, volume mount and dismount events, new drive letters, filesystem writes with unusual volume or timing, and command line tools or scripting engines touching a removable path. The honest detection problem is that legitimate staff also copy large files to USB drives, so volume alone is weak. Useful differentiation comes from correlation: a burst of file reads across many shares or user directories followed within minutes by a write to a removable volume, an upload that happens outside working hours, or a device with no prior history on that host. Where endpoint logging is thin, physical controls, port policy and asset records carry much of the weight.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker copies stolen data onto a USB stick or USB hard drive. They do this instead of sending it over the network. USB means Universal Serial Bus, the standard port you use for keyboards and memory sticks. It is a sub-technique of Exfiltration Over Physical Medium. The difference is simple. Here the data travels in someone's pocket rather than down a cable to the internet.
beginner.whyItMatters: Many teams guard the network and forget the ports on the desk. A network sensor cannot see data that walks out of the building on a keyring. This matters most on isolated networks, where a USB stick may be the only way in or out. If nobody watches device connections, a large theft can look like an ordinary file copy.
howItWorks: The attacker collects the files they want and gathers them into one place, often a temporary folder.
They insert a USB storage device into a computer that holds the data. The operating system mounts it as a new drive.
They copy the gathered files onto that device. This may take minutes and produces a large write to a removable volume.
They remove the device and carry it to another machine, or out of the building completely.
For an isolated network, the same device may move data between systems. Those systems never connect to each other.
The victim's own staff are sometimes the bridge. A trusted person plugs in an unknown device, or one they found.
beginner.example: Picture a hospital at night. A cleaner with a master key can walk into any records room and fill a shopping bag with paper files. Then they leave through the staff entrance. Cameras cover the front door, but nobody checks the side corridor or the bag. The files never went by fax or email, so the phone records look normal. The only clues are a door log and a bag that was empty on the way in.
takeaways: Data can leave a network without using the network at all.
Device connection logs are the main evidence, so make sure they are collected.
Large copies to removable drives are worth reviewing, not automatically blocking.

objectives: Explain why USB exfiltration is the main data loss path for air-gapped networks.
Describe how a removable device is mounted, written to and removed, and what each step records.
Identify the host telemetry that shows a device connection and a large write to removable media.
Distinguish a hostile copy from a legitimate backup or file transfer by correlating staging and timing.
List the physical and policy controls that reduce the risk when logging is incomplete.
